title: Incident Response
description: The incident response process: events versus incidents, then preparation, triage, action and investigation, and recovery with lessons learned.

nodes.title: Prep.
nodes.description:
Groundwork done before any incident, so the organization can respond effectively when one happens.
Examples: write an incident response policy and procedures, identify and train the right people, and put monitoring capabilities in place.

nodes.title: Triage
nodes.description:
The high-level bucket that starts the response once something happens: work out whether an incident is occurring, then mobilize the response team and assess how bad it is.
Incident response aims to detect incidents, respond effectively and efficiently to reduce the impact on the organization, maintain or restore business continuity, and defend against future attacks.
Many incident response processes exist, such as NIST's, with slightly different numbers and names of steps. Do not focus too much on the exact steps and names. They all share the same goals: be prepared, detect and respond quickly, minimize the damage, return to normal operations, and learn from it to improve and prevent future incidents.

children.title: Detection
children.description:
The first and absolutely most important step. If you cannot spot an incident, you cannot activate the incident response process or do any of the other steps.
On the exam, if asked to put the incident response steps in order, always look for Detection as the first step.

children.title: Sources
children.description:
Ways to identify and detect incidents in the flood of events that keep happening:
- SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) systems, fed by tools such as intrusion detection systems
- IDS/IPS (Intrusion Detection / Prevention Systems)
- DLP (Data Loss Prevention)
- Fire detectors, and other building monitoring systems such as fire alarms
- Etc., for example a report from an employee

children.title: Event
children.description:
An observable occurrence.
Examples: someone logging in, a file being written to a drive, someone scanning the external firewall.
Most events are not of particular concern.

children.title: Incident
children.description:
An adverse event: an event that negatively impacts the organization in some way.
Examples: a server crashing, a password being brute forced, an attacker getting through the firewall.
Incidents definitely matter.

children.title: Response (IR Team Deployed)
children.description:
Once an incident is detected, activate the incident response team.
One of the team's first tasks is an impact assessment: how severe the incident is and how long recovery will take. The impact assessment drives the rest of the process.
If the Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) will be exceeded, it is no longer treated as an incident: declare a disaster and enact the BCP or DRP.

nodes.title: Action / Investigation
nodes.description: The middle bucket of incident response: limit the damage, find out what happened, and keep the relevant stakeholders informed.

children.title: Mitigation (Containment)
children.description:
Minimize the damage and stop the incident from spreading.
Examples: if a worm is spreading across the network, disconnect systems from the network; if there is a fire, activate the fire suppression system.

children.title: Reporting (Relevant Stakeholders)
children.description:
Reporting actually happens throughout the incident response process.
One dedicated contact person on the incident response team keeps all relevant stakeholders informed (management, investors, regulators, customers, the media and so on), so the rest of the team can stay focused on responding.

nodes.title: Recovery
nodes.description: The last bucket: get things back to business as usual, and make improvements so the same incident does not happen again.

children.title: Recovery (Return to normal)
children.description:
Bring things back to business as usual.
Examples: eradicate the worm and reconnect systems to the network; after a fire, clean up the charred, soaking office, install new carpet, paint the walls and move in new furniture.

children.title: Remediation (Prevention)
children.description:
Actually begins in parallel with mitigation.
Root cause analysis to find out how to stop the problem from recurring, for example to stop the worm spreading while systems are recovered, or to stop the fire reigniting.
Continues through recovery and the closure of the incident, and leads into lessons learned.

children.title: Lessons Learned (Improve Process)
children.description:
The post-incident step: how did this happen, and how can we prevent it from happening again?
The goal is to make processes and systems better and to teach people, so future incidents are prevented, or are detected more quickly and handled more effectively if they do happen.
